862.title: Baba Deep Singh the scholar
862.hook: before his last ride, tradition says he spent years copying the Granth at Damdama
862.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Damdama Sahib at Talwandi Sabo as a seat of Sikh learning, and remember Baba Deep Singh both as a copyist of the Guru Granth Sahib and as a martyr.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an Afghan king came through Punjab again and again, and the Khalsa kept rising in chardi kala. Your line was again and again. A new week begins at a quiet desk.

A lamp, a low desk, a sheet of paper, a pot of ink, a reed pen. An old man bends over the page and forms one Gurmukhi letter, then the next. Outside, Punjab is full of horsemen and burning villages. In here it's quiet, except for the scratch of the pen. Sikhs know how Baba Deep Singh's story ends: the old warrior on his last ride to Amritsar. This lesson stays with the years before it, at the desk.
screen: `A LAMP, A REED PEN, A PAGE.` → `ONE LETTER, THEN THE NEXT.` → `BEFORE THE LAST RIDE.`

segments.voice: The place was Damdama Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo, in the dry south of Punjab. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh stayed there after years of war, and that the Granth was written out there in its full form, with Bhai Mani Singh as scribe and Baba Deep Singh beside him. Tradition says Baba Deep Singh stayed on after the Guru left, teaching, and copying the Granth by hand so more sangats could have it. There's no printing press. Every copy of the Guru's word is made one letter at a time, and a slip of attention puts a word wrong. So the copyist has to be slow, steady and humble before the text, for years. Guru Nanak has a line about writing that fits this desk exactly. In paraphrase, from the Granth: burn away worldly attachment and grind it into ink; make your understanding the paper; make love the pen and the mind the writer; then ask the Guru, and write the Name. For Guru Nanak that's a picture of the inner life. At Damdama it was also an actual workday. Then look at his hands. The same hands that held the pen would later hold a sword. Sikhs call people like him scholar-warriors, and they don't treat the two halves as a contradiction. The Khalsa's ideal, in a phrase Sikhs use, is sant-sipahi, saint-soldier. Baba Deep Singh's last ride makes sense because of the desk. He knew exactly what the Harmandir and the Guru's word meant, letter by letter, because he had copied it. The scholar-warrior.

segments.voice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, write out one line from your own tradition's scripture, or, if you don't have one, the opening words of the Granth: Ik Oankar, one God. Write it slower than feels natural, each letter a whole breath, and notice your attention when your hand has to be careful. If you pray, say Waheguru as you set the pen down.
Sant-sipahi, saint-soldier, the Khalsa's ideal that Baba Deep Singh lived at Damdama Sahib, the same hands that held the pen later holding the sword.
Your line: the scholar-warrior. Slow, careful work can be the ground courage stands on. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

863.title: The pool filled in
863.hook: invaders filled the Harmandir's pool with rubbish, and Sikhs vowed to restore it
863.howItsDone: Sikhs walk around the sarovar at the Harmandir Sahib and some bathe at its steps, and the pool has been cleaned in later times by kar seva, with volunteers carrying out silt by hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baba Deep Singh at his desk at Damdama, copying the Granth letter by letter. Your line was the scholar-warrior. Today, the news that reached that desk.

The water comes first. At the Harmandir there's a wide pool, still and bright, with the temple sitting in the middle of it and its reflection beneath. People walk all the way around; some bathe at the steps. The whole place is built around that water. Now take the water away. Tradition says that when Abdali's commanders held Amritsar, they had the pool filled in with rubbish, earth and filth, and the sacred place was defiled. A messenger rides south with the news.
screen: `A STILL, BRIGHT POOL.` → `THE TEMPLE IN THE MIDDLE.` → `THEN THE RUBBISH.`

segments.voice: Start with what the pool is. Tradition says Guru Ram Das began digging it, and Guru Arjan finished the work and built the Harmandir in its center. Tradition also says the city took its name from it: Amritsar, the pool of amrit, the water of immortality. And Guru Arjan sang about it. In a hymn in the Granth, in paraphrase, he says that God himself stood up to finish the work of his saints, and that the land is lovely and the pool is lovely, filled with nectar-water. So the pool isn't decoration. In Sikh memory it's the Gurus' own work, made by hand and blessed in song. Tradition reads the filling as a message: this is over. The Sikh answer was a vow. Tradition says that when the news reached Damdama, Baba Deep Singh, yesterday's old scholar, swore to free the Harmandir, and set out. Leave the ride for another time; stay with what came after the vow. Restoring a pool isn't one dramatic act. It's baskets. People standing in mud, passing rubble hand to hand, carrying it out, again and again, until the water can come back. Sikhs call that shared physical work for the Guru's house kar seva, the service of the hands. And Sikhs tell of the pool being cleaned by kar seva in later times too, with ordinary people, young and old, carrying out silt in baskets. The vow and the basket belong together. One says it will be made right. The other makes it right, one load at a time. Restore it.

864.title: Freeing the captives, 1761
864.hook: after Panipat, Sikh horsemen freed women being taken away by Abdali's army and returned them home
864.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of the freed captives in gurdwara talks as an example of the Khalsa's duty to protect the defenseless, alongside the teaching that a Sikh regards other women as mothers, sisters and daughters.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pool at the Harmandir filled with rubbish, and a vow that turned into baskets. Your line was restore it. Today, people carried home.

Here's a question that sounds easy until it's real. You've just pulled someone out of danger. They're frightened, far from home, and for the moment completely in your hands. What happens next? Tradition says Sikh riders faced exactly that after a great battle at Panipat, which Abdali's army had won. Heading home to Afghanistan, the army took captive women with it, and Sikh horsemen struck and set them free. The raid is the famous part. The tradition dwells on what came after it.
screen: `A RESCUE, AND THEN WHAT?` → `PANIPAT, AND AN ARMY HEADING HOME.` → `THE PART AFTER THE RAID.`

segments.voice: Last week, Sikh riders struck a departing Persian army and walked its captives home. This story asks a harder question: what kind of men were the rescuers, once the rescue was done? Tradition says Sikh horsemen fell on the rear of Abdali's army as it crossed the rivers of Punjab, and freed the women it was taking away. The Sikhs had no stake in that battle at Panipat. These weren't their wives or their sisters. They rode anyway. Then came the real test. Once free, the women were in the hands of armed men in a lawless time, far from home. Anything could have happened. Tradition says the Sikhs gave them food and escort, and took them back to their own families. Not kept. Not claimed. Brought home. Why does the tradition make so much of that? Because Sikh tradition measures the Khalsa by how it treats the defenseless. Bhai Gurdas, describing the true Sikh in his Vars, says, in paraphrase, that when he sees other people's women, he looks on them as mothers, sisters and daughters. That was the standard. For the women in the story, it meant something very concrete: a door opening in their own village, and their own people standing in it. Notice the order of the story. The freeing was quick. The bringing home took long walking, care and restraint. Freedom is the start. Brought home safe is the finish.

865.title: Kup Rahira, February 1762
865.hook: in the great holocaust, the Khalsa formed a moving ring round its families, and very many died
865.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust fought near Kup and Rahira, in the Ardas and at commemorations, honoring those who died shielding the families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women carried off after Panipat were freed and walked back to their own families. Your line was brought home safe. Today, families of their own, and a hard day.

For years the Khalsa had stayed alive by being fast. A band of horsemen could strike and be gone before an army turned around. Speed was their shelter. Now look at the column crossing the fields near two villages called Kup and Rahira. It isn't fast at all. It's carts and cattle and grandparents and children, moving at the pace of the slowest walker. Riding alongside are fighters who have lived by speed, going slow on purpose. Then an army appears.
screen: `SPEED WAS THEIR SHELTER.` → `A COLUMN AT A WALKING PACE.` → `THE FAST RIDE SLOW.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call a moving camp of families like this a vahir: children, elders, the cooking pots, everything. The great holocaust has been told before: the surprise, the ring, the terrible losses. Today, look at one choice inside that day. When Abdali's army caught the vahir, the fighters had a way out. Horsemen can scatter; they'd done it for years. Split up, ride hard, regroup later. Some of them might have got away. Tradition says they didn't. They formed a ring around the families, fought on the outside, and kept the whole column moving forward together, at the pace of its slowest people. Riders would turn and charge to push the attackers back, then return to the ring, again and again, all day. That's what a shield is. Not the strongest thing on the battlefield, but the thing that stays between the danger and the ones who can't run. The cost was enormous. Very many died that day, fighters and families both. This lesson gives no figure. It remembers the people. Why stay? Sikh teaching holds that the Khalsa is there to protect the defenseless, and these weren't strangers. They were mothers, fathers, children. The Ardas, said at the close of gurdwara gatherings, remembers those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith, and Sikhs hold the dead of Kup Rahira among the ones it carries. It's not a story with a clever twist. It's a story about staying. The fast rode slow, and they shielded the families.

866.title: The temple destroyed
866.hook: Abdali blew up the Harmandir; tradition says a flying brick struck his nose
866.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the destruction of the Harmandir by Ahmad Shah Abdali as part of the eighteenth-century persecutions, and teach that the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib and the Guru Panth, not any building.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kup Rahira: fighters who lived by speed rode slow, ringing their families. Your line was they shielded the families. Today, the Guru's house itself.

Barrels are carried across the causeway to the Harmandir, the temple in the middle of the pool. Gunpowder. They're packed inside, among the walls where the Granth's hymns had been sung morning and evening. The Sikh families who might have stood there are dead or scattered after Kup Rahira. Ahmad Shah Abdali has come to Amritsar. The fuse is lit. Then the blast, and the stones and bricks fly. Tradition adds a detail Sikhs still tell: a brick flew from the explosion and struck Abdali on the nose.
screen: `GUNPOWDER ON THE CAUSEWAY.` → `THE BLAST.` → `A BRICK STRIKES THE KING.`

segments.voice: Don't hurry past the loss. The Harmandir was the Gurus' house, built in the pool Guru Arjan had finished, where the Granth had been installed. Now it was rubble, and tradition says the pool was filled in again. For Sikhs who heard the news, it came on top of the dead at Kup Rahira. The building fell. That's the line, and it's meant to be said plainly. Now the brick. Tradition says the wound on Abdali's nose never properly healed, and some tellings say it troubled him for the rest of his life. That link belongs to the story, not to a record. Sikhs tell it not as a joke and not quite as a miracle, but as a sign that what's done to the Guru's house doesn't simply go away. So what did Sikhs say was lost, and what wasn't? Guru Gobind Singh, before his death, had said the Guru from then on would be the Granth, the scripture, and the Panth, the community of the Khalsa. Sikhs say neither could be blown up with a building. That doesn't make the loss small. People had prayed in that room; their parents had prayed there. But it changes what kind of loss it is. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a line in the Granth, in paraphrase: whatever has been made will pass away, today or tomorrow. The Sikh scripture doesn't promise that buildings last. It points past them. So today, just sit with what fell. What comes next is tomorrow's story.

Harimandar, the house of God. Ahmad Shah Abdali had it blown up with gunpowder, and tradition says a flying brick struck him on the nose; the building fell, but Sikhs say the Guru did not. Today's word.
Your line: the building fell. A loss can be real and still not be the end. Until tomorrow.

867.title: Diwali at the ruins
867.hook: months later the Sikhs gathered at Amritsar again and began to rebuild
867.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Diwali as Bandi Chhor Divas, and at Amritsar the Harmandir Sahib and its pool are lit with lamps; the story of gathering at the ruins is told in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an invading army blew up the Harmandir. Your line was the building fell. Today, what the Sikhs did next.

Lamps along a broken wall. That's the scene tradition keeps. The Harmandir is rubble, and the pool around it has been fouled and filled. The army that did it is still in Punjab, and the families who survived the great killing earlier that year are still burying people. Then the season of Diwali comes round, the festival of lamps, and Sikhs start arriving in Amritsar. Not a few. Riders, families, whole bands, coming to the ruins on the day they have always come.
screen: `THE HARMANDIR IN RUBBLE.` → `THE SEASON OF LAMPS COMES ROUND.` → `SIKHS RIDE BACK TO AMRITSAR.`

segments.voice: Why Diwali? For Sikhs, Diwali at Amritsar had long been a time to gather, as Vaisakhi was in spring. It's tied in Sikh memory to Guru Hargobind coming home to Amritsar after being released from prison, the day many Sikhs now call Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release. So the date already meant coming back to the Guru's city after a time of captivity. They came on purpose, on the day that means homecoming. Then, what they found: no building to gather in. Tradition says they gathered anyway, at the place itself, because the place was never only the bricks. And what they did: they began clearing. Cleaning the pool. Taking the first stones of a new beginning. Guru Arjan's hymn about the pool, the one this path heard four days ago, comes back here, in paraphrase: the Lord himself stood up to complete the work of the saints. Some Sikhs sing it when new work begins, and it's easy to hear why it fit that autumn. The work wasn't theirs alone. Tradition also says Abdali's army, still in Punjab, fell on the gathering that season and there was fighting at Amritsar, so this was no quiet festival. Rebuilding the Harmandir fully took years. But the beginning was a crowd of people with lamps at a ruin, refusing to let the day pass unmarked. Begin again.
screen: `DIWALI: THE DAY OF RELEASE AND HOMECOMING.` · `NO BUILDING, AND THEY GATHERED ANYWAY.` · `CLEARING THE POOL, THE FIRST STONES.` · `THE LORD STANDS UP TO FINISH THE WORK.` · then, large: `BEGIN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit with something that broke, a plan, a habit, a friendship, and don't try to fix the whole of it; the Sikhs at Amritsar didn't rebuild a temple that night, they lit lamps and moved some stones. Ask only what the first stone is, one message, one drawer cleared, one page, and stay with it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
Diwali, the festival of lamps. After the Harmandir was destroyed, tradition says the Sikhs gathered at Amritsar for it anyway, and began clearing the pool and rebuilding. Today's word.
Your line: begin again. Nobody rebuilds a temple in a night. Day eight hundred sixty-seven, lamps lit.

868.title: Sirhind, 1764
868.hook: the Dal Khalsa took Sirhind and the land of Punjab passed to the Sikh confederacies
868.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the fall of Sirhind in Sikh histories, and gather at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib, where the younger Sahibzade died, to remember them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lamps at a broken Harmandir, and the first stones moved. Your line was begin again. Today, a city with a long shadow.

Sirhind. This path has stood here before. Once in grief, at the wall where the Guru's youngest sons were put to death on the governor's order. And once with Banda Singh Bahadur's forces, who took the city years later. Then the city passed out of Sikh hands again, and the hard decades you've been hearing about came down. Now the riders of the Dal Khalsa are outside its walls once more.
screen: `THE WALL WHERE THE SAHIBZADE DIED.` → `TAKEN BY BANDA, THEN LOST.` → `THE DAL KHALSA AT THE GATES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The story comes in three movements. First, the taking. Tradition says the bands of the Dal Khalsa came together against Sirhind and defeated its governor, who was killed in the fighting. For Sikhs, this wasn't just another town on the map. It was the place their memory kept circling back to. Second, what they did with the city. Tradition says Sikhs treated Sirhind as a place under a shadow, and that for a long time Sikhs passing by would take a brick from its ruins and throw it in the river. Some tellings call it the city the Guru's curse fell on. And at the spot where the young Sahibzade died, Sikhs marked the ground; a gurdwara called Fatehgarh Sahib stands there now. Its name carries the name of the younger of the two, Fateh Singh, and fateh means victory. The place of the children's deaths bears a word for victory. Third, the land. After Sirhind, the territory around it was divided among the Sikh confederacies, the misls, each band holding its own share. In this telling, the chiefs stop being hunted riders and start holding the countryside. Bands who had once hidden in forests and deserts now held the villages. That's the turn, and nothing about the hard decades had promised it. The persecutions, the great killing, the temple blown up: people at Sirhind remembered all of it. And here, at the city where the smallest martyrs died, the tide turned.
screen: `THE DAL KHALSA TAKES SIRHIND.` · `A BRICK THROWN IN THE RIVER.` · `FATEHGARH: FATEH SINGH'S NAME, A WORD FOR VICTORY.` · `THE LAND PASSES TO THE MISLS.` · then, large: `THE TIDE TURNED.`

segments.voice: Look back over your own life and find one moment when something changed direction: a phone call, a door that opened, a day you stopped doing something, or started. It may not have looked like much at the time; hold it in mind, and notice what came before it, and how long the before lasted. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

Sirhind. The city of the Sahibzade's deaths, taken by the Dal Khalsa, after which the land passed to the misls. This week: Baba Deep Singh, the pool filled in, captives home, Kup Rahira, the temple destroyed, Diwali at the ruins, and Sirhind. Today's word.
Your line: the tide turned. Turns are easy to miss while they happen. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.
